title: Constitutional Bodies
shortDescription: Six independent institutions the Constitution itself creates — elections, recruitment, finance, audit, and legal advice.
genZNote: The Constitution's own hand-picked watchdogs — can't be shut down by an ordinary law, only by amending the Constitution itself.

sections.heading: Constitutional vs. Statutory Bodies
sections.body: This distinction is a favourite exam trap, so it's worth locking in first.

rows: A provision of the Constitution itself
An ordinary Act of Parliament or a State Legislature
A simple legislative amendment or repeal
Election Commission, UPSC, Finance Commission, CAG
National Human Rights Commission, Central Vigilance Commission (both statutory); NITI Aayog (a non-statutory executive resolution body, neither constitutional nor an Act-based statutory body)

sections.heading: Election Commission of India (Article 324)
bullets: Vested with the 'superintendence, direction and control' of elections to Parliament, State Legislatures, and the offices of President and Vice President.

A permanent, independent body functioning since 1950; originally a single-member body, it became multi-member in 1989 and now consists of the Chief Election Commissioner (CEC) plus 2 Election Commissioners.
Tenure: 6 years, or until the age of 65, whichever is earlier.

The CEC can be removed only in the same manner as a Supreme Court judge (parliamentary impeachment-style process); the other Election Commissioners can be removed by the President on the CEC's recommendation — giving the CEC more security of tenure than the other two.

sections.heading: Union Public Service Commission and State Public Service Commissions (Articles 315–323)
bullets: UPSC conducts examinations for appointments to All India Services and Central Civil Services, and advises the Government on recruitment and disciplinary matters; the Chairman and members are appointed by the President.

Tenure: 6 years, or until the age of 65, whichever is earlier; removable by the President, but only after the Supreme Court, on a reference, holds an inquiry and reports misbehaviour (Article 317) — a safeguard for independence.

State Public Service Commissions (SPSCs) perform the equivalent role for State services; their members are appointed by the Governor, but — notably — can be removed ONLY by the President, not the Governor, even though the Governor appoints them. Tenure: 6 years, or until the age of 62.

sections.heading: Finance Commission (Article 280)
sections.body: Constituted by the President every 5 years (or earlier if needed), consisting of a Chairman and 4 other members. Its core job is to recommend: (a) the distribution of net proceeds of taxes between the Union and the States, and among the States themselves; (b) the principles governing grants-in-aid to States; and (c) measures needed to strengthen the resources of Panchayats and Municipalities (added after the 73rd and 74th Amendments), to supplement their own funds.

sections.heading: Comptroller and Auditor General of India (Articles 148–151)
bullets: Often called the 'guardian of the public purse' — audits all expenditure from the Consolidated Fund of India and of every State, and the accounts of many government companies and corporations.
Appointed by the President; tenure of 6 years, or until the age of 65, whichever is earlier.
Removed only in the same manner and on the same grounds as a Supreme Court judge.
Reports on the Union's accounts are submitted to the President, and on a State's accounts to that State's Governor; each report is then laid before the relevant legislature.
Dr. B.R. Ambedkar described the CAG as 'the most important officer under the Constitution'.

sections.heading: Attorney General of India (Article 76) and Advocate General of a State (Article 165)
bullets: The Attorney General is the highest law officer of the Union, appointed by the President, and must be qualified to be appointed a Supreme Court judge.

Unlike a typical full-time government law officer, the Attorney General is not a government servant and is permitted to engage in private legal practice; there is no fixed tenure — the office is held during the pleasure of the President.
The Attorney General has the right to speak and take part in proceedings of both Houses of Parliament (and their committees), but no right to vote there.
The Advocate General plays the equivalent role for a State, appointed by the Governor, and must be qualified to be appointed a High Court judge.

quickRevision.oneLineDefinition: Constitutional bodies (Election Commission, UPSC/SPSC, Finance Commission, CAG, Attorney General/Advocate General) are created directly by the Constitution and can be changed only by amending it.
keyFacts: Election Commission (Art 324) became multi-member (CEC + 2 ECs) in 1989.
Finance Commission (Art 280) is constituted every 5 years by the President.
CAG (Art 148) is called the 'guardian of the public purse'; removed like a Supreme Court judge.
State PSC members are appointed by the Governor but removable only by the President.
commonConfusion: The National Human Rights Commission and NITI Aayog are commonly mistaken for constitutional bodies — neither is; the NHRC is statutory, and NITI Aayog is a non-statutory executive resolution body, not created by the Constitution at all.

highYieldFacts: Dr. B.R. Ambedkar called the CAG 'the most important officer under the Constitution'.
The Attorney General of India is not a full-time government servant and may engage in private practice — unusual for a top law officer.
A State Public Service Commission member is appointed by the Governor but can be removed only by the President, not the Governor.
commonTraps: Do not classify the National Human Rights Commission (NHRC) as a constitutional body — it is statutory, created by an Act of Parliament (the Protection of Human Rights Act, 1993), not by the Constitution.

Do not say the CEC and other Election Commissioners have identical removal protection — only the CEC is protected like a Supreme Court judge; the other Election Commissioners are removed by the President on the CEC's recommendation.
mustRemember: Election Commission, UPSC, SPSC, Finance Commission, CAG, Attorney General, and Advocate General are all constitutional bodies.
A constitutional body can be abolished or restructured only through a constitutional amendment — never by ordinary legislation.

confusedTerms.distinction: A constitutional body (e.g. Election Commission, CAG) is created directly by the Constitution and needs a constitutional amendment to change; a statutory body (e.g. NHRC, CVC) is created by an ordinary Act and can be changed by ordinary legislation.
